dsm5_criteria.criteria_a: Five (or more) of the following symptoms have been present during the same 2-week period and represent a change from previous functioning; at least one of the symptoms is either (1) depressed mood or (2) loss of interest or pleasure.
symptoms: Depressed mood most of the day, nearly every day
Markedly diminished interest or pleasure in all, or almost all, activities most of the day
Significant weight loss when not dieting or weight gain, or decrease or increase in appetite nearly every day
Insomnia or hypersomnia nearly every day
Psychomotor agitation or retardation nearly every day
Fatigue or loss of energy nearly every day
Feelings of worthlessness or excessive or inappropriate guilt
Diminished ability to think or concentrate, or indecisiveness
Recurrent thoughts of death, recurrent suicidal ideation without a specific plan, or a suicide attempt or a specific plan for committing suicide
dsm5_criteria.duration: Symptoms must persist for at least 2 weeks
dsm5_criteria.severity: Symptoms cause clinically significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning
dsm5_criteria.exclusion: Symptoms are not attributable to the physiological effects of a substance or another medical condition

Major Depressive Disorder.icd10_code: F32.x (Major depressive disorder, single episode), F33.x (Major depressive disorder, recurrent)
clinical_pearls: Screen for bipolar disorder - ask about previous manic or hypomanic episodes
Anhedonia and early morning awakening are particularly suggestive of melancholic depression
Women are 1.5-2x more likely to develop MDD than men
Family history of depression increases risk 2-4 fold
Symptoms must represent a change from previous functioning
Seasonal pattern suggests seasonal affective disorder
Postpartum depression can occur within 4 weeks of delivery
common_pitfalls: Missing medical causes: thyroid disease, B12 deficiency, autoimmune disorders
Failing to assess for substance use as primary cause
Not screening for suicide risk adequately
Confusing grief with major depression - grief symptoms decrease in intensity over time
Underestimating the impact of chronic medical conditions
Not considering bipolar disorder in treatment-resistant depression
red_flags: Suicidal ideation or plan (immediate safety assessment required)

management.moderate: Combination of psychotherapy and antidepressant medication
management.severe: Antidepressant medication + psychotherapy, consider ECT if psychotic features
management.maintenance: Continue medication for 6-12 months after remission

dsm5_criteria.criteria_a: Depressed mood for most of the day, for more days than not, for at least 2 years.
symptoms: Poor appetite or overeating
Insomnia or hypersomnia
Low energy or fatigue
Low self-esteem
Poor concentration or difficulty making decisions
Feelings of hopelessness
dsm5_criteria.duration: At least 2 years (1 year in children/adolescents)
dsm5_criteria.severity: Not better explained by other disorders
dsm5_criteria.exclusion: Not attributable to substances or medical conditions

clinical_pearls: Often begins in adolescence or early adulthood
Patients may not remember being asymptomatic
Poor treatment response compared to major depression
High rate of comorbid personality disorders
Often preceded by childhood trauma or adversity
Risk for developing major depressive episodes
common_pitfalls: Missing the chronic nature of symptoms
Underestimating functional impairment
Not assessing for early-onset personality disorders
Failing to recognize comorbid substance use
Expecting rapid treatment response

management.psychotherapy: CBT or IPT for at least 1 year

dsm5_criteria.criteria_a: Emotional or behavioral symptoms in response to an identifiable stressor within 3 months of onset of the stressor.
symptoms: Depressed mood
Anxiety
Worry
Inability to plan or continue in situation
dsm5_criteria.duration: Symptoms resolve within 6 months after stressor ends
dsm5_criteria.exclusion: Not better explained by other disorders

clinical_pearls: Symptoms develop within 3 months of stressor
Stressor is usually identifiable
Symptoms are disproportionate to the stressor
Common after relationship breakups, job loss, health issues
Generally good prognosis with proper support
common_pitfalls: Missing the temporal relationship with stressor
Not assessing stressor's impact adequately
Over-medicating when support is needed
Failing to provide adequate psychosocial interventions

management.support: Address stressors and build coping skills

dsm5_criteria.manic_episode: Distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood and abnormally and persistently increased activity or energy lasting at least 1 week (or any duration if hospitalization is necessary)
dsm5_criteria.hypomanic_episode: Distinct period of abnormally and persistently elevated, expansive, or irritable mood and abnormally and persistently increased activity or energy lasting at least 4 consecutive days and present most of the day, nearly every day
dsm5_criteria.depressive_episode: Same criteria as major depressive episode, but in context of history of manic or hypomanic episode

clinical_pearls: Ask specifically about previous manic or hypomanic episodes
Sleep deprivation can precipitate manic episodes
Family history of bipolar disorder is strong risk factor
First episode often depression - miss bipolar diagnosis
Seasonal pattern may be present
Substance use common comorbidity
common_pitfalls: Missing hypomanic episodes in depression treatment
Not asking about sleep, energy, and goal-directed activity
Misdiagnosing bipolar depression as unipolar depression
Underestimating suicide risk in bipolar disorder
Not assessing for rapid cycling
red_flags: History of manic or hypomanic episodes

management.depression: Mood stabilizers + psychotherapy, avoid antidepressants alone
management.psychosocial: Psychoeducation, family therapy, social rhythm therapy

dsm5_criteria.criteria_b: At least one of the attacks has been followed by 1 month (or more) of one or both of the following: (1) Persistent concern or worry about additional panic attacks or their consequences; (2) A significant maladaptive change in behavior related to the attacks.
dsm5_criteria.exclusion: Not attributable to physiological effects of a substance or another medical condition

clinical_pearls: Panic attacks are discrete episodes that peak within 10 minutes
Physical symptoms can be severe and mimic medical emergencies
Patients often fear having a heart attack or going crazy
Interoceptive conditioning perpetuates the disorder
Agoraphobia commonly develops
Lifetime prevalence is 2-3%
common_pitfalls: Missing agoraphobia development
Not providing adequate education about panic attacks
Focusing only on symptoms without addressing avoidance
Not assessing for other anxiety disorders
Missing medical causes (thyroid, cardiac)

management.benzodiazepines: Short-term use only due to dependence risk

dsm5_criteria.criteria_a: Excessive anxiety and worry (apprehensive expectation), occurring more days than not for at least 6 months, about a number of events or activities.
symptoms: Restlessness or feeling keyed up or on edge
Being easily fatigued
Difficulty concentrating or mind going blank
Irritability
Muscle tension
Sleep disturbance
dsm5_criteria.severity: Difficult to control worry, causes impairment
dsm5_criteria.exclusion: Not attributable to substances or medical conditions

clinical_pearls: Worry is pervasive and difficult to control
Multiple areas of life affected
Physical symptoms often prominent
Often comorbid with depression or other anxiety disorders
Family history of anxiety disorders common
Childhood onset may indicate chronic course
common_pitfalls: Missing the 6-month duration requirement
Not assessing functional impairment adequately
Overlooking medical causes
Focusing only on symptoms without understanding worry pattern
Not considering comorbid conditions

management.psychotherapy: CBT with worry exposure and cognitive restructuring
management.lifestyle: Regular exercise, sleep hygiene, stress management

dsm5_criteria.criteria_a: Presence of obsessions, compulsions, or both.
dsm5_criteria.obsessions: Recurrent and persistent thoughts, urges, or images that are intrusive and unwanted, causing anxiety or distress; individual attempts to ignore or suppress them or neutralize them with some other thought or action.
dsm5_criteria.compulsions: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts that the individual feels driven to perform in response to an obsession or according to rigid rules; behaviors aimed at reducing anxiety or preventing some dreaded event.
dsm5_criteria.duration: Time-consuming or causes clinically significant distress or impairment
dsm5_criteria.exclusion: Not attributable to substances or medical conditions

clinical_pearls: Insight can range from good to absent
Common comorbid conditions: depression, tic disorders, eating disorders
Early onset (before age 10) often indicates tic-related OCD
Hoarding now separate disorder but can be comorbid
Body dysmorphic disorder often comorbid
common_pitfalls: Missing subthreshold symptoms that cause impairment
Not assessing insight level
Confusing perfectionism with OCD
Underestimating time spent on rituals
Missing comorbid tic disorders

management.first_line: CBT with exposure and response prevention (ERP)
management.medication: SSRIs at higher doses than depression
management.severe: Consider deep brain stimulation in extreme cases

dsm5_criteria.criteria_a: A pervasive pattern of instability of interpersonal relationships, self-image, and affects, and marked impulsivity beginning by early adulthood and present in a variety of contexts.
symptoms: Frantic efforts to avoid real or imagined abandonment
A pattern of unstable and intense interpersonal relationships
Identity disturbance
Impulsivity in at least two areas (spending, sex, substance use, reckless driving, binge eating)
Recurrent suicidal behavior, gestures, or threats, or self-mutilating behavior
Affective instability due to marked reactivity of mood
Chronic feelings of emptiness
Inappropriate, intense anger
Transient, stress-related paranoid ideation or severe dissociative symptoms
dsm5_criteria.exclusion: Not better explained by other disorders

clinical_pearls: Emotional dysregulation is core feature
Fear of abandonment often drives behavior
Splitting (black-and-white thinking) common
Self-harm often non-suicidal but high risk
Therapeutic relationship can be challenging
Dialectical behavior therapy most effective treatment
common_pitfalls: Missing comorbid conditions (depression, PTSD, substance use)
Not recognizing self-harm as non-suicidal
Avoiding therapy due to challenging behavior
Not addressing trauma history
Expecting rapid improvement
red_flags: Suicidal ideation with plan and means
